key_insight: At Re = 1000, a hemispherical leading-edge protuberance advances vortex-shedding onset to 5° angle of attack, while a simple flat plate achieves better glide ratios at 5°, 10°, and 15°.
engineering_relevance: Leading-edge geometry can inform aerodynamic trade-offs for small unmanned aerial or aquatic vehicles operating at low Reynolds numbers.
method: Two-dimensional numerical flow simulations at Re = 1000.
Compare a simple flat plate with a plate featuring a hemispherical leading-edge protuberance.
Evaluate vortex shedding, shedding frequencies, and aerodynamic forces over 0°–25° angle of attack.
evidence_signal: Simulations show thicker vortical regions near the modified plate, delayed shedding onset for the simple plate, and multiple temporal force-coefficient frequencies at higher angles of attack.
watch_item: Results are limited to two-dimensional simulations at one Reynolds number; applicability to three-dimensional vehicle flows requires further validation.
paper_title: Effect of leading edge geometry on aerodynamic performance of a flat plate
